newsitem.title: USA: IBM's Richard Thoman takes No. 2 spot at Xerox.
newsitem.headline: IBM's Richard Thoman takes No. 2 spot at Xerox.

text.p: Xerox Corp. on Thursday named G. Richard Thoman, International Business Machines Corp.'s No. 2 executive, as president and chief operating officer, making him heir apparent to Xerox Chairman and Chief Executive Paul Allaire.

Thoman, 52, joined IBM in 1994 and was named chief financial officer in 1995. He is widely credited with turning around IBM's personal computer business and was well-liked by Wall Street analysts in his most recent position as CFO.

Thoman will report directly to Xerox's Allaire in a newly formed Office of the Chairman. Thoman is clearly in line to eventually take over the world's best-known copier company, but he said it is a position he has to earn.

"I have always had a dream of running a company and when I learned of this opportunity, Paul and I began to talk," Thoman said in a phone interview. "Xerox is an icon of American business and I thought it was an opportunity I wasn't going to see again. ... I came to Xerox to have the opportunity to become CEO. But it's a job I have to earn."
Allaire, 58, said he has no plans to step down anytime soon but that Stamford, Conn.-based Xerox has a tradition of its CEOs stepping down at age 60. Allaire turns 59 in July.

"My expectation is that I'd be around the company for a few more years and there would be a transition to the CEO," Allaire said. He said Thoman will strengthen Xerox's management team and brings a fresh perspective to lead the company into the 21st century.

Armonk, N.Y.-based IBM said its senior vice president and chief counsel, Lawrence Ricciardi, would assume Thoman's responsibilities on an interim basis. He will continue to be responsible for IBM's legal, government and intellectual property functions.

The sudden departure of Thoman is not seen as a major negative for the computer giant, analysts said. They said IBM is in better financial shape and a much stronger company than when Jerome York, Thoman's predecessor, left in 1995, and its stock tumbled on the news.
"The major challenges are behind it, they are not ahead," said Jay Stevens, at Buckingham Research Group. "Jerry York laid the groundwork and Thoman came in and kept it going."
York was the first CFO under CEO Louis Gerstner, who joined in April 1993 to turn the then-troubled IBM around.
Ricciardi, 56, said he and Gerstner tried to persuade Thoman to stay when he informed them of his decision late last Friday evening.
"Obviously, he has always wanted to run a public company and he viewed this as a wonderful opportunity," Ricciardi told Reuters. "We'd love to have kept him here."
Ricciardi said he has worked with Thoman for more than 20 years in various positions, including when they both worked for Gerstner at both RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. and at American Express Co.
Ricciardi said it was too early to tell whether he will remain as IBM's chief financial officer on a permanent basis, or whether IBM will begin to look for a new CFO.
"We haven't had time to sort through this," he said. "Lou and I will sit down and look at the functions and do whatever makes the most sense for IBM."

On the New York Stock Exchange, IBM closed up $1 at $88.25 on volume of about 3,150,000 shares. The shares had traded as low was $85.50 during the day and fell immediately following news of Thoman's departure.
Xerox shares rallied on the news, jumping to as high as $73.25 before settling back to close up $2 at $71.75 on volume of about 2,320,000 shares on the NYSE.

"It's a super deal for Xerox," B. Alex Henderson, a Prudential Securities analyst, said of Thoman's move. "He turned around the PC division at IBM and has exceptional operational credentials. Xerox needed to fill this post and wanted to fill it with somebody from the outside. To bring in IBM blue blood is a fabulous move."

Thoman is the second chief financial officer to leave since Gerstner became chairman of the giant computer maker. Jerome York, the previous chief financial officer, left IBM to work for billionaire Kirk Kerkorian's Tracinda Corp.
